
=== PAGE 1 ===
01
Introduction
to
Robotics
WHAT
IS
ROBOTICS?
Why
it
matters:
Before
you
build
a
robot,
you
need
to
know
what
makes
something
a
robot
and
not
just
a
machine.
Robotics
deals
with
the
design,
construction,
operation,
and
use
of
robots.
It
also
covers
the
computer
systems
that
control
them,
give
them
sensory
feedback,
and
process
their
information.
A
robot
is
an
automatically
operated
machine
that
replaces
human
effort.
Two
things
set
a
robot
apart:
●
It
can
perform
autonomously,
without
a
person
controlling
every
move.
●
It
can
carry
out
repetitive
instructions
with
precision
and
accuracy,
doing
the
same
task
many
times
and
doing
it
well
each
time.
Notice
that
precision
and
accuracy
show
up
in
the
deﬁnition
of
a
robot
itself.
That’s
why
they’re
one
of
Acamad’s
Technical
Standards
(T04).
BASIC
PARTS
OF
A
ROBOT
Every
robot,
from
a
classroom
line
tracer
to
a
factory
arm,
is
built
from
the
same
four
groups
of
parts.
If
you
know
the
groups,
you
know
where
to
look
when
something
goes
wrong.
Part
What
it
does
Think
of
it
as
Mechanical
The
parts
that
move
The
body
Actuation
Moves
the
mechanical
parts
(e.g.,
motors)
The
muscles
Sensory
Connects
the
robot
to
its
environment
The
senses
Control
Processes
information
and
makes
decisions
The
brain
These
four
groups
depend
on
each
other.
The
sensors
gather
information,
the
controller
decides
what
to
do
with
it,
and
the
actuators
move
the
mechanical
parts.
If
one
group
fails,
the
whole
robot
fails.
That’s
the
idea
of
integration
you’ll
see
again
in
T03
(Functionality).
Example:
A
line-tracing
robot
uses
sensors
to
detect
the
line,
a
controller
to
decide
which
way
to
steer,
motors
(actuation)
to
turn
the
wheels,
and
a
chassis
and
wheels
(mechanical)
to
move
across
the
ﬁeld.
1

=== PAGE 2 ===
TYPES
OF
ROBOTS
Where
a
robot
works
decides
how
it
should
be
built.
●
Industrial
robots
are
used
in
factories
to
automate
production
lines.
They
operate
at
high
precision
and
speed.
●
Field
robots
are
non-factory
robots,
usually
mobile,
that
operate
in
complex
and
changing
environments.
2

=== PAGE 3 ===
●
Service
robots
work
closely
with
humans
to
help
them
in
their
daily
lives.
ROBOTICS
PLATFORMS
AND
COMPETITIONS
Knowing
the
platforms
and
competitions
helps
you
see
what
kind
of
robot
you’ll
be
building,
and
with
what
tools.
Common
robotics
platforms:
●
Arduino
●
INEX
ATX
●
VEX
●
LEGO
●
Roborobo
3

=== PAGE 4 ===
Common
robotics
competitions:
●
Sumobot:
robots
try
to
push
each
other
out
of
a
ring
●
Line
Tracing:
robots
follow
a
line
on
the
ﬁeld
●
Mission
Challenge:
robots
complete
a
set
of
tasks
on
a
ﬁeld
●
Innovative
Challenge:
teams
build
a
project
that
solves
a
problem
(the
Creative
side)
●
Fireﬁghting:
robots
ﬁnd
and
put
out
a
ﬂame
●
Robot
Soccer:
robots
play
a
soccer
match
Most
of
these
are
Technical
competitions,
judged
by
how
well
the
robot
performs.
The
Innovative
Challenge
belongs
to
the
Creative
side.
You’ll
learn
the
standards
for
both
in
Section
02.
4

=== PAGE 5 ===
5

=== PAGE 6 ===
02
Acamad’s
Robotics
Standards
UNDERSTANDING
COMPETITIVE
ROBOTICS
The
Two
Sides
of
Competitive
Robotics
When
people
think
of
robotics
competitions,
they
usually
picture
robots
racing,
pushing,
or
picking
up
objects
on
a
ﬁeld.
That’s
one
side.
But
there’s
another
side
just
as
important.
The
Technical
side
is
about
performance
and
engineering.
These
are
the
traditional
robot
games:
a
ﬁeld,
a
set
of
tasks,
a
scoring
system,
and
robots
built
to
complete
those
tasks
as
well
as
possible.
The
question
here
is:
How
well
does
this
robot
perform?
The
Creative
side
is
about
innovation
and
research.
Here,
you
design
a
robotics
project
that
solves
a
real
problem
or
explores
a
new
possibility.
The
question
here
is:
Is
this
idea
worth
building,
and
is
it
built
on
solid
thinking?
These
two
sides
are
not
separate
worlds.
A
strong
creative
project
still
needs
good
engineering
to
work,
and
technical
teams
still
need
creative
thinking
to
design
clever
solutions.
They
overlap
and
support
each
other.
What
is
a
Standard?
A
standard
is
a
deﬁned
criterion
used
to
judge
the
quality
or
performance
of
robotics
work.
Instead
of
saying
“this
robot
looks
good”
or
“this
project
seems
cool,”
standards
give
you
speciﬁc
things
to
check.
Each
side
has
ﬁve
standards:
Technical
Standard:
1.
Proportionality
2.
Stability
&
Balance
3.
Functionality
4.
Precision
&
Accuracy
5.
Consistency
Creative
Standard:
1.
Value
2.
Feasibility
3.
Credibility
4.
Logic
5.
Consistency
6

=== PAGE 7 ===
Why
the
Order
Matters?
The
standards
are
sequential.
Each
one
builds
on
the
ones
before
it.
Think
of
it
like
building
a
house:
you
don’t
paint
the
walls
before
the
foundation
is
poured.
On
the
Technical
side:
●
If
materials
are
badly
distributed
(Proportionality),
weight
ends
up
uneven.
●
If
weight
is
uneven
(Stability),
the
robot
tips
or
drifts,
and
it
can’t
do
its
job.
●
If
it
can’t
do
its
job
(Functionality),
there’s
no
point
measuring
how
exactly
it
does
it.
●
If
it
isn’t
exact
(Precision
&
Accuracy),
it
can’t
be
reliable.
●
Only
after
all
that
can
you
ask:
does
it
do
this
every
single
time?
(Consistency)
Notice
that
Consistency
is
last
on
both
sides.
It’s
the
ﬁnal
proof
that
the
work
is
reliable
after
everything
before
it
is
in
place.
One
more
key
idea:
evaluate
work
using
the
right
standards.
Don’t
judge
a
creative
research
project
only
by
how
fast
its
robot
drives,
and
don’t
judge
a
competition
robot
by
how
original
the
idea
is.
Common
Mistakes
●
“Technical
and
Creative
robotics
are
completely
separate.”
→
They
overlap
and
support
each
other.
●
“A
robot
only
needs
to
work
to
be
successful.”
→
Working
is
only
one
standard
out
of
ﬁve.
●
“A
project
is
innovative
just
because
the
idea
is
new.”
→
A
new
idea
still
has
to
prove
its
value
and
pass
the
Creative
standards.
●
“I
can
check
the
standards
in
any
order.”
→
Later
standards
depend
on
earlier
ones.
T01
-
PROPORTIONALITY
Why
it
matters:
How
you
place
parts
on
your
robot
decides
almost
everything
that
comes
after:
its
weight,
its
balance,
and
how
well
it
performs.
Proportionality
is
the
equal
or
appropriate
distribution
of
materials
throughout
a
robot,
according
to
its
design
requirements.
Two
words
in
that
deﬁnition
are
worth
slowing
down
for:
●
Materials
means
the
physical
parts
and
substances
used
to
build
the
robot:
the
battery,
motors,
controller,
frame,
and
so
on.
●
Appropriate
means
“right
for
this
robot’s
purpose.”
It
does
not
mean
“identical.”
7

=== PAGE 8 ===
A
proportional
robot
doesn’t
need
every
part
to
be
the
same
size,
amount,
or
shape.
A
robot
built
to
lift
objects
will
place
its
parts
differently
from
a
robot
built
for
speed,
and
both
can
be
proportional.
What
matters
is
that
the
distribution
makes
sense
for
the
design.
Proportionality
also
means
no
unnecessary
material.
If
a
part
doesn’t
help
the
robot
do
its
job,
it’s
adding
weight
and
taking
up
space
for
nothing.
Tool:
The
Quadrant
Check
1.
Look
at
your
robot
from
the
top
view.
2.
Imagine
two
perpendicular
lines
crossing
at
the
center
of
the
chassis.
This
splits
it
into
four
quadrants:
front-left,
front-right,
back-left,
back-right.
3.
List
what
components
sit
in
each
quadrant.
4.
For
each
component
on
one
side
of
a
line,
look
at
the
opposite
side.
Is
there
something
that
keeps
the
distribution
appropriate?
5.
If
one
quadrant
holds
a
big
component
and
the
opposite
quadrant
is
empty,
stop
and
ask:
Does
the
design
actually
need
it
this
way?
Example:
Your
battery
sits
in
the
front-left
quadrant.
Now
look
at
the
front-right.
Is
it
empty?
Does
that
make
sense
for
your
robot,
or
should
something
be
rearranged?
Important:
The
Quadrant
Check
is
a
guideline,
not
a
rule.
Components
don’t
have
to
be
identical
or
perfectly
mirrored.
Sometimes
an
uneven
layout
is
intentional.
The
point
is
that
you
chose
it
for
a
reason.
Key
terms
●
Design
requirement:
a
condition
the
robot’s
design
must
satisfy.
●
Distribution:
how
materials
or
components
are
arranged
throughout
the
robot.
●
Material:
a
physical
substance
or
component
used
to
build
the
robot.
Common
mistakes
●
“Proportional
means
every
part
is
the
same
size.”
●
“Parts
must
be
identical
or
symmetrical
on
opposite
sides.”
●
“Proportionality
and
Stability
are
the
same
thing.”
→
Proportionality
is
about
materials.
Stability
is
about
weight.
You’ll
see
the
difference
next
lesson.
T02
-
STABILITY
&
BALANCE
Why
it
matters:
A
robot
that
tilts,
wobbles,
or
tips
over
can’t
complete
tasks,
no
matter
how
good
its
code
is.
Stability
&
Balance
is
about
the
appropriate
distribution
of
weight
throughout
the
robot.
8

=== PAGE 9 ===
Here’s
how
this
connects
to
Proportionality:
Proportionality
asks
where
are
the
materials?
Stability
asks
where
is
the
weight?
Two
parts
of
the
same
size
can
weigh
very
different
amounts.
A
battery
and
a
sensor
might
take
up
similar
space,
but
the
battery
is
much
heavier.
So
a
robot
can
look
evenly
laid
out
and
still
be
badly
balanced.
The
Center
of
Gravity
(CoG)
The
Center
of
Gravity
is
the
point
where
the
robot’s
total
weight
can
be
considered
to
act.
It’s
like
the
robot’s
“balance
point.”
Key
facts
about
the
CoG:
●
It
sits
closer
to
where
most
of
the
mass
is.
Heavy
parts
pull
it
toward
them.
●
It’s
not
automatically
the
center
of
the
chassis.
It
depends
on
the
mass
and
placement
of
every
component.
●
A
higher
CoG
makes
a
robot
more
likely
to
tip
or
move
in
unwanted
ways.
Taller
robots
often
have
higher
CoGs.
The
Base
of
Support
The
base
of
support
is
the
area
enclosed
by
the
robot’s
points
of
contact
with
the
ground
(for
example,
its
wheels).
A
wider
base
generally
means
more
stability.
Think
of
how
you
stand
on
a
moving
bus.
You
naturally
spread
your
feet
apart
and
bend
your
knees.
Spreading
your
feet
widens
your
base
of
support.
Bending
your
knees
lowers
your
center
of
gravity.
Robots
follow
the
same
idea.
Stability
isn’t
only
about
standing
still.
Weight
distribution
matters
most
when
the
robot
is
moving:
turning,
accelerating,
and
stopping
suddenly.
A
robot
that’s
ﬁne
while
parked
can
still
tip
during
a
sharp
stop.
Counterweights
are
weights
added
on
purpose
to
adjust
weight
distribution
and
improve
balance.
Tool:
Estimating
the
CoG
1.
Identify
heavy
components:
battery,
motors,
and
other
heavy
parts.
2.
Observe
their
placement:
Is
most
of
the
weight
on
one
side?
Near
the
top?
3.
Estimate
the
CoG:
It
will
be
closer
to
where
the
mass
is
concentrated.
4.
Adjust:
Move
heavy
parts
lower
and
distribute
weight
better.
Example:
If
the
battery
and
motors
are
both
on
the
left
side,
the
CoG
is
probably
closer
to
the
left.
Moving
some
of
that
weight
can
improve
balance.
9

=== PAGE 10 ===


=== PAGE 11 ===
●
Functionality:
the
ability
to
perform
an
intended
purpose.
●
Integration:
connecting
mechanical,
electrical,
and
software
components
so
they
work
together.
Common
mistakes
●
“If
the
robot
moves,
it’s
functional.”
●
“If
it
worked
once,
it’s
fully
functional.”
T04
-
PRECISION
&
ACCURACY
Why
it
matters:
In
competitions,
“close
enough”
often
isn’t.
Points
depend
on
hitting
exact
positions
and
targets.
These
two
words
are
often
used
as
if
they
mean
the
same
thing.
In
robotics,
they
don’t.
●
Accuracy
is
how
close
a
result
is
to
the
intended
target.
●
Precision
is
how
close
repeated
results
are
to
each
other.
The
dartboard
picture.
Imagine
throwing
four
darts:
What
happens
Precise?
Accurate?
All
four
land
in
a
tight
group,
right
on
the
bullseye
✅
✅
All
four
land
in
a
tight
group,
but
in
the
corner
of
the
board
✅
❌
One
lands
on
the
bullseye,
the
others
scatter
everywhere
❌
Only
that
once
All
four
scatter
randomly
❌
❌
So:
●
A
robot
can
be
precise
without
being
accurate:
it
gets
the
same
result
every
time,
but
consistently
misses
the
target.
●
A
robot
can
be
accurate
once
without
being
precise:
it
hits
the
target
on
one
try,
but
its
results
vary
across
tries.
This
is
why
one
trial
tells
you
almost
nothing.
You
need
repeated
trials
to
know
whether
a
robot
is
precise.
What
affects
precision
and
accuracy?
It
isn’t
just
the
code.
Precision
and
accuracy
can
be
affected
by:
●
Mechanical
alignment
●
Sensor
readings
11

=== PAGE 12 ===
●
Motor
control
●
Programming
●
Environmental
conditions
(lighting,
temperature,
the
surface
the
robot
drives
on)
Because
the
environment
matters,
test
in
conditions
similar
to
where
the
robot
will
compete.
Testing
and
calibration
help
you
ﬁnd
and
reduce
these
errors.
(Calibration
gets
its
own
lesson
next.)
Tool:
The
Precision
&
Accuracy
Check
1.
Choose
a
target,
such
as
stopping
at
a
marked
line.
2.
Run
repeated
trials.
3.
Record
the
results.
Measure
in
centimeters
or
millimeters.
4.
Identify
the
issue:
○
Results
close
together
but
all
missing
the
target
→
precise,
not
accurate
○
Results
spread
far
apart
→
lacks
precision
5.
Adjust
and
retest.
Look
into
programming,
sensors,
mechanical
alignment,
and
the
environment.
Example:
A
robot
is
programmed
to
stop
at
a
line.
It
stops
2
cm
before
the
line
in
every
trial.
That’s
precise,
but
not
accurate.
If
it
stopped
at
a
different
distance
each
time,
its
precision
would
be
poor.
Key
terms
●
Accuracy:
how
close
a
result
is
to
the
intended
or
correct
value.
●
Calibration:
adjusting
or
verifying
a
device’s
measurements
or
output
against
a
known
reference.
●
Deviation:
the
difference
between
an
observed
result
and
the
intended
value.
●
Error:
the
difference
between
the
actual
result
and
the
expected
result.
●
Precision:
how
close
repeated
results
are
to
one
another.
Common
mistakes
●
“Precision
and
accuracy
mean
the
same
thing.”
●
“Hitting
the
target
once
means
the
robot
is
precise
and
accurate.”
●
“Programming
alone
controls
precision
and
accuracy.”
→
Mechanics,
sensors,
motors,
calibration,
and
the
environment
matter
too.
●
“I
only
need
to
calibrate
once.”
T05
-
CONSISTENCY
Why
it
matters:
In
a
competition,
you
don’t
get
to
choose
which
run
counts.
Your
robot
has
to
perform
when
it
matters,
every
time.
12

=== PAGE 13 ===
Consistency
is
the
robot’s
ability
to
produce
reliable
and
repeatable
results
across
multiple
attempts
under
similar
conditions.
It
comes
last
for
a
reason.
Consistency
is
the
proof
that
everything
before
it
holds
up:
the
layout,
the
balance,
the
function,
and
the
precision.
Consistency
doesn’t
mean
perfection.
Small
variations
are
normal.
The
goal
is
performance
that’s
repeatable
enough
for
the
task.
If
your
robot
needs
to
stop
within
a
scoring
zone,
a
few
millimeters
of
difference
between
runs
may
not
matter.
Where
inconsistency
comes
from
It’s
tempting
to
blame
the
code
every
time.
But
inconsistent
performance
can
come
from
four
areas:
●
Mechanical:
loose
screws,
wobbly
parts,
misaligned
wheels
●
Electrical:
loose
or
inconsistent
connections
●
Sensor-related:
readings
that
change
between
runs
●
Software:
programming
issues
Fix
the
cause,
not
the
symptom.
Recalibrating
before
every
run
might
help
for
a
while,
but
it
hides
the
real
problem.
If
something
keeps
drifting,
ﬁnd
out
why.
Tool:
The
Consistency
Check
1.
Choose
a
task
you
can
repeat:
drive
a
set
distance,
turn,
pick
up
a
game
piece.
2.
Repeat
it
several
times
with
the
same
program
and
setup.
3.
Observe.
Does
the
robot
do
the
same
sequence
of
actions
with
similar
results
every
time?
4.
Identify
variations
in
movement,
timing,
sensor
responses,
or
mechanisms.
5.
Investigate.
Check
for
loose
components,
inconsistent
connections,
changing
sensor
readings,
or
code
issues.
6.
Retest
after
each
adjustment.
Example:
Your
robot
is
programmed
to
drive
forward
and
turn
at
a
speciﬁc
point.
If
it
completes
the
sequence
every
time,
it’s
consistent.
If
it
turns
correctly
in
some
runs
but
misses
the
turn
in
others,
investigate
why.
Key
terms
●
Consistency:
producing
similar
results
repeatedly
under
similar
conditions.
●
Reliability:
performing
intended
functions
dependably
over
time.
●
Repeatability:
achieving
similar
results
when
the
same
procedure
is
repeated
under
the
same
conditions.
●
Variation:
a
difference
in
results
across
attempts.
●
Troubleshooting:
identifying
and
resolving
the
causes
of
problems
in
a
system.
13

=== PAGE 14 ===
Common
mistakes
●
“Inconsistency
is
always
a
programming
problem.”
●
“Recalibrating
before
every
run
is
the
only
way
to
improve
consistency.”
●
“Consistency
means
identical
results
every
time.”
14

=== PAGE 15 ===
03
Basic
Electronics
Every
robot
runs
on
electricity.
Before
a
robot
can
move,
sense,
or
think,
its
circuits
have
to
be
built
correctly.
A
single
wrong
connection
can
stop
a
robot
or
destroy
a
component.
VOLTAGE,
CURRENT,
AND
RESISTANCE
Three
quantities
describe
every
circuit:
●
Voltage
(V):
the
electrical
“push”
that
moves
current
through
a
circuit.
Measured
in
volts
(V).
●
Current
(I):
the
ﬂow
of
electricity
through
a
circuit.
Measured
in
amperes
(A).
●
Resistance
(R):
how
much
a
component
limits
the
ﬂow
of
current.
Measured
in
ohms
(Ω).
Think
of
water
in
a
pipe.
Voltage
is
the
water
pressure,
current
is
how
much
water
ﬂows,
and
resistance
is
how
narrow
the
pipe
is.
More
pressure
pushes
more
water.
A
narrower
pipe
lets
less
water
through.
THE
BREADBOARD
(PROTOBOARD)
A
breadboard
is
used
for
prototyping
and
testing
electronic
circuits.
It
lets
you
build
and
change
circuits
quickly,
without
soldering
components
together.
You
make
connections
using
jumper
wires.
How
the
holes
are
connected
The
holes
on
a
breadboard
aren’t
all
separate.
Inside,
metal
strips
connect
certain
holes:
●
Power
rails:
the
long
rows
along
the
top
and
bottom
edges,
usually
marked
red
(+)
and
blue
(−).
All
the
holes
in
one
rail
are
connected
horizontally,
along
the
length
of
the
board.
Use
them
to
share
power
and
ground
across
your
circuit.
●
Body
(Terminal
strips):
the
main
area
in
the
middle.
Holes
are
connected
vertically
in
short
groups
of
ﬁve.
Each
group
is
a
separate
connection.
●
Center
gap:
the
channel
down
the
middle.
It
separates
the
top
and
bottom
halves,
so
the
groups
on
either
side
are
not
connected.
Example:
If
you
put
a
resistor
leg
and
an
LED
leg
in
the
same
vertical
group
of
ﬁve,
they’re
connected.
Move
the
LED
one
column
over,
and
they’re
not.
15

=== PAGE 16 ===
TYPES
OF
CIRCUITS
There
are
two
basic
ways
to
connect
components:
Series
circuit:
components
are
connected
one
after
another,
in
a
single
path.
The
same
current
ﬂows
through
every
component.
●
If
one
component
breaks
or
is
removed,
the
path
is
broken
and
everything
stops.
●
Example:
a
battery,
one
resistor,
and
one
LED
connected
in
a
single
loop.
Parallel
circuit:
components
are
connected
on
separate
branches,
each
with
its
own
path
back
to
the
power
source.
●
If
one
branch
breaks,
the
other
branches
keep
working.
●
Example:
a
9
V
battery
powering
three
branches,
each
with
its
own
resistor
and
LED.
Tool:
Trace
the
Path
Put
your
ﬁnger
on
the
positive
terminal
of
the
power
source
and
follow
the
wire.
If
there’s
only
one
route
back
to
negative,
it’s
series.
If
the
route
splits
into
branches,
it’s
parallel.
16

=== PAGE 17 ===
RESISTORS
Without
a
resistor,
too
much
current
can
rush
through
a
component
and
destroy
it.
A
resistor
is
a
two-terminal
electrical
component
that
limits
the
ﬂow
of
current.
It
controls
the
voltage
and
current
in
a
circuit,
which
keeps
components
like
LEDs
from
being
damaged
by
too
much
current.
Resistance
is
measured
in
ohms
(Ω).
A
resistor’s
value
is
shown
using
colored
bands.
Each
color
represents
a
number.
Tool:
Reading
a
4-Band
Resistor
Hold
the
resistor
so
the
gold
or
silver
band
is
on
the
right.
Read
from
left
to
right:
1.
Band
1:
ﬁrst
digit
2.
Band
2:
second
digit
3.
Band
3:
multiplier
(how
many
zeros
to
add)
4.
Band
4:
tolerance
(how
far
the
actual
value
may
vary)
Example:
Brown,
Red,
Red,
Gold
●
Brown
=
1,
Red
=
2
→
12
●
Red
multiplier
=
×
100
→
12
×
100
=
1,200
Ω
●
Gold
=
±5%
●
Value:
1,200
Ω
±5%
(also
written
1.2
k
Ω)
Note:
Most
resistors
have
4
bands.
For
almost
all
of
your
circuits,
you
can
ignore
the
4th
(tolerance)
band.
Some
resistors
have
5
bands:
three
digit
bands,
then
the
multiplier,
then
the
tolerance.
17

=== PAGE 18 ===
LIGHT-EMITTING
DIODE
(LED)
An
LED
is
a
type
of
diode
that
emits
light
when
current
ﬂows
through
it.
Polarity:
LEDs
only
work
one
way
An
LED
has
two
legs,
and
they’re
not
interchangeable:
●
Anode
(+):
the
longer
leg.
It
connects
toward
the
positive
side.
●
Cathode
(−):
the
shorter
leg.
It
connects
toward
the
negative
side.
The
cathode
side
of
the
LED’s
rim
also
has
a
ﬂat
spot.
If
you
connect
an
LED
backward,
it
won’t
light
up.
Safety
rules
●
Always
connect
an
LED
with
a
resistor
in
series.
●
NEVER
connect
an
LED
directly
to
a
battery
or
power
supply.
Without
a
resistor,
too
much
current
ﬂows
and
the
LED
can
burn
out.
Uses:
status
indicators,
digital
displays,
lighting
systems
18

=== PAGE 19 ===


=== PAGE 20 ===
●
Pressed:
completes
the
circuit
(closes
the
switch),
so
current
ﬂows.
●
Unpressed:
opens
the
circuit,
so
current
stops.
●
Uses:
control
systems
(keyboards,
doorbells),
start/stop
functions,
user
interactions
Self-locking
push
button:
each
press
toggles
between
two
states,
and
it
stays
in
the
new
state
until
you
press
it
again.
●
On:
locked
●
Off:
unlocked
●
Uses:
toggle
switches
(light
switches),
safety
systems
(ﬁre
alarms,
elevator
buttons)
20

=== PAGE 21 ===
Tool:
Which
Button
Do
I
Need?
Ask:
Should
the
action
stop
the
moment
I
let
go?
●
Yes
→
momentary
(a
doorbell
rings
only
while
pressed)
●
No,
it
should
stay
on
until
I
press
again
→
self-locking
(a
light
switch
stays
on)
STEPS
IN
BUILDING
YOUR
CIRCUIT
A
messy
breadboard
is
hard
to
check
and
even
harder
to
ﬁx.
If
you
build
every
circuit
the
same
way,
you’ll
spot
mistakes
faster,
and
so
will
anyone
helping
you.
The
two
parts
of
the
breadboard
●
Power
rail:
the
long
rows
along
the
top
and
bottom
edges,
marked
red
(+)
and
blue
(−).
This
is
where
power
comes
in
and
gets
shared.
●
Body:
the
main
area
in
the
middle,
where
you
place
your
components
and
make
your
connections.
Reading
positions:
letter,
then
number
The
body
has
letters
for
rows
(A
to
J)
and
numbers
for
columns
(1,
2,
3,
…).
You
name
a
hole
by
its
letter
ﬁrst,
then
its
number,
like
A30.
Use
these
labels
to
place
components
and
to
describe
your
circuit
to
others.
“Put
the
LED’s
anode
in
C12”
is
much
clearer
than
“put
it
near
the
middle.”
Remember
how
the
body
is
connected
(E03):
holes
in
the
same
numbered
column
on
the
same
side
of
the
center
gap
are
connected.
A30
to
E30
are
connected
to
each
other.
F30
to
J30
are
a
separate
group,
across
the
gap.
Initial
Conﬁguration
Most
circuits
start
with
this
same
setup:
1.
Connect
the
battery
to
the
positive
(+)
and
negative
(−)
rails
at
the
top
left
of
the
breadboard.
2.
Connect
the
top
right
rails
to
the
bottom
right
rails,
matching
polarity:
top
+
to
bottom
+,
top
−
to
bottom
−.
Now
both
the
top
and
bottom
rails
have
power,
so
you
can
reach
positive
and
negative
from
anywhere
on
the
board.
Start
with
this
conﬁguration
most
of
the
time.
21

=== PAGE 22 ===
Connect
your
components:
Top
to
Bottom,
Left
to
Right
Place
and
connect
components
in
order,
top
to
bottom
and
left
to
right,
the
same
way
you
read
a
page.
This
keeps
your
circuit
organized.
You
(and
your
facilitator)
can
follow
it
like
reading,
and
it’s
easy
to
see
where
each
part
of
the
circuit
begins
and
ends.
Follow
the
Resistor
First
convention
Place
the
resistor
on
the
positive
side
of
the
component:
Power
(+)
→
Resistor
→
LED
anode
(long
leg)
→
LED
cathode
(short
leg)
→
GND
(−)
The
LED’s
cathode
then
connects
straight
to
the
negative
rail.
Note:
A
resistor
on
the
negative
side
also
works,
because
in
a
series
circuit
the
same
current
ﬂows
through
every
component.
You
may
see
it
that
way
in
other
guides.
At
Acamad,
we
use
Resistor
First
so
every
circuit
is
built
and
checked
the
same
way.
22

=== PAGE 23 ===
Tool:
The
Finger
Trace
(Troubleshooting)
When
your
circuit
doesn’t
work:
1.
Put
your
index
ﬁnger
on
the
positive
power
rail.
2.
Follow
the
connection
to
the
ﬁrst
component.
Imagine
the
current
ﬂowing
through
it.
3.
Keep
tracing
from
one
component
to
the
next,
the
way
current
would
ﬂow,
until
you
reach
the
negative
rail.
4.
At
each
component,
check:
○
Is
it
in
the
right
hole
(letter
and
number)?
○
Is
it
connected
to
the
next
component
through
the
same
column?
○
Is
the
polarity
correct
(anode
toward
positive,
cathode
toward
negative)?
5.
Make
sure
every
component
that
needs
both
polarities
has
a
positive
and
a
negative
connection.
If
your
ﬁnger
can’t
get
from
+
to
−
through
a
component,
current
can’t
either.
Example:
You
trace
from
the
+
rail
to
the
resistor
in
B10,
then
to
the
LED
anode
in
C10,
then
the
LED
cathode
in
C11...
and
column
11
never
reaches
the
−
rail.
Current
has
nowhere
to
go,
so
the
LED
stays
off.
Add
a
jumper
wire
from
column
11
to
the
negative
rail.
23

=== PAGE 24 ===
04
Introduction
to
Arduino
Programming
ARDUINO
HARDWARE
In
Section
03,
a
person
controlled
the
circuit
by
pressing
buttons
and
turning
knobs.
With
a
microcontroller,
code
controls
it.
This
is
the
robot’s
control
system:
its
brain.
An
Arduino
board
is
built
around
a
microcontroller,
a
small
computer
on
a
chip
that
runs
your
program.
Key
parts
of
the
board:
●
USB
port:
connects
the
board
to
your
computer
for
power
and
uploading
code
●
USB-to-serial
chip:
handles
communication
between
the
computer
and
the
microcontroller
●
Microcontroller:
runs
your
program
●
Digital
pins:
for
digital
input
and
output
●
Analog
pins
(A0,
A1,
…):
for
reading
analog
input
●
Power
pins:
5V,
3.3V,
GND
(ground),
and
VIN
BASIC
OPERATION
Three
things
to
know
about
how
an
Arduino
runs:
1.
Most
Arduino
boards
are
designed
to
run
one
program
at
a
time
on
the
microcontroller.
2.
The
program
starts
running
as
soon
as
the
board
is
powered.
3.
The
program
runs
incredibly
fast,
generally
within
microseconds,
unless
you
tell
it
to
slow
down.
(The
exact
speed
depends
on
the
size
of
the
program
and
how
long
the
microcontroller
takes
to
execute
it.)
That
third
point
matters.
If
you
blink
an
LED
with
no
pause,
it
switches
so
fast
that
it
looks
like
it’s
always
on.
That’s
why
we
use
delay().
ARDUINO
IDE
AND
SKETCHES
The
Arduino
IDE
is
the
software
you
use
to
write
code
and
upload
it
to
the
board.
Download
it
from
www.arduino.cc/en/software.
A
sketch
is
the
ﬁle
you
write
your
program
in.
It
has
the
.ino
extension
and
is
always
stored
in
a
folder
with
the
same
name.
Program
structure
Every
Arduino
program
needs
at
least
two
functions:
24

=== PAGE 25 ===
void
setup()
●
Runs
only
once,
when
the
Arduino
is
powered
on
or
reset.
●
This
is
where
you
conﬁgure
things,
like
setting
a
pin
as
input
or
output,
setting
the
baud
rate
of
serial
communication,
or
starting
a
library.
void
loop()
●
Runs
over
and
over
for
as
long
as
the
board
has
power.
●
This
is
where
your
main
program
goes,
like
turning
a
lamp
on
or
off
based
on
an
input,
or
taking
a
sensor
reading
every
few
seconds.
BLINK
Tool:
Uploading
a
Sketch
1.
Prepare
your
circuit.
Connect
an
LED
and
a
resistor
using
the
5V,
GND,
and
D13
(digital
pin
13)
pins.
2.
Have
your
circuit
checked
by
a
facilitator
before
continuing.
3.
Create
a
new
sketch:
File
→
New
Sketch
(Ctrl+N).
4.
Write
the
code.
5.
Verify
your
sketch
(the
✓
button).
This
checks
your
code
for
errors.
6.
Choose
the
correct
board
and
port:
Select
Other
Board
and
Port,
then
pick
your
board
and
the
port
it’s
connected
to.
7.
Upload
your
sketch
(the
→
button).
The
code
void
setup
()
{
pinMode
(
13
,
OUTPUT
);
}
void
loop
()
{
digitalWrite
(
13
,
HIGH
);
delay
(
1000
);
digitalWrite
(
13
,
LOW
);
delay
(
1000
);
}
What
each
line
does
●
pinMode(13,
OUTPUT);
sets
pin
13
to
behave
as
an
output.
It
goes
inside
setup()
because
it
only
needs
to
happen
once.
●
digitalWrite(13,
HIGH);
sends
a
HIGH
signal
to
pin
13,
which
turns
the
LED
on.
●
delay(1000);
pauses
the
program
for
1,000
milliseconds
(1
second).
●
digitalWrite(13,
LOW);
sends
a
LOW
signal
to
pin
13,
which
turns
the
LED
off.
25

=== PAGE 26 ===
●
Then
loop()
starts
over,
so
the
LED
keeps
blinking:
on
for
1
second,
off
for
1
second.
ELECTRONIC
SIGNALS:
ANALOG
&
DIGITAL
Sensors
and
actuators
talk
to
the
Arduino
in
one
of
two
“languages.”
You
need
to
know
which
one
each
component
uses.
Digital
signals
A
digital
signal
has
only
two
states:
0
or
1,
read
as
LOW
or
HIGH.
Think
of
a
light
switch:
it’s
either
off
or
on.
●
digitalRead(pin)
reads
the
state
of
a
digital
pin
(HIGH
or
LOW).
●
digitalWrite(pin,
value)
writes
a
HIGH
or
LOW
state
to
a
digital
pin.
●
Examples:
a
push
button
(pressed
or
not),
an
LED
that’s
simply
on
or
off.
Analog
signals
An
analog
signal
can
take
any
value
within
a
range.
On
an
Arduino,
that
range
is
usually
0–5
V
(or
0–3.3
V
on
some
boards).
Think
of
a
dimmer:
it
can
be
anywhere
between
off
and
full
brightness.
●
analogRead(pin)
reads
the
value
from
an
analog
pin
and
returns
a
number
from
0
to
1023.
●
analogWrite(pin,
value)
writes
a
value
from
0
to
255
to
a
pin.
●
Examples:
a
potentiometer
(any
position
between
its
ends),
an
LED
that
fades.
Note:
analogWrite()
only
works
on
pins
marked
with
a
~
symbol
on
the
board,
such
as
pin
9.
26

=== PAGE 27 ===
Tool:
Digital
or
Analog?
Ask:
Does
this
only
have
two
states,
or
can
it
be
anywhere
in
between?
●
Two
states
→
digital
●
Anywhere
in
a
range
→
analog
READING
CODE:
POTENTIOMETER-CONTROLLED
LED
Being
able
to
read
code
and
ﬁgure
out
what
it
does
is
just
as
important
as
writing
it.
int
potValue
=
0
;
void
setup
()
{
pinMode
(
9
,
OUTPUT
);
}
void
loop
()
{
potValue
=
analogRead
(
A0
);
analogWrite
(
9
,
potValue
/
4
);
delay
(
10
);
}
What
it
does:
It
reads
the
value
of
a
potentiometer
and
adjusts
an
LED’s
brightness
based
on
it.
What
each
line
does
●
int
potValue
=
0;
creates
a
variable
called
potValue
to
store
a
whole
number,
starting
at
0.
●
pinMode(9,
OUTPUT);
sets
pin
9
(where
the
LED
is
connected)
as
an
output.
●
potValue
=
analogRead(A0);
reads
the
potentiometer
on
analog
pin
A0
and
stores
the
result
(0
to
1023).
●
analogWrite(9,
potValue
/
4);
sets
the
LED’s
brightness
on
pin
9.
●
delay(10);
pauses
for
10
milliseconds
before
reading
again.
27

=== PAGE 28 ===
Why
divide
by
4?
analogRead()
gives
a
value
from
0
to
1023,
but
analogWrite()
only
accepts
0
to
255.
Dividing
by
4
scales
the
range
to
ﬁt:
1023
÷
4
≈
255.
28
